claim: In Claude Code the skill listing truncates each skill's combined description and when_to_use text at 1,536 characters, so the key use case must come first.
why: The cap exists to reduce context usage of the always-loaded listing, and text past it is not seen by Claude when routing.
check: Measure description plus when_to_use per skill; flag any over 1,536 characters or with the trigger condition buried late.
quote: the combined `description` and `when_to_use` text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing to reduce context usage

claim: The Claude Code skill listing has a character budget of 1% of the model's context window; when it overflows, descriptions of the least-invoked skills are dropped first while all names stay.
why: Dropped descriptions remove the keywords Claude needs to match a request, so a large skill set silently degrades routing.
check: Count installed skills and total description size; if the listing likely overflows, flag the set as too large or recommend name-only overrides or pruning.
quote: The budget scales at 1% of the model's context window. When the listing overflows, Claude Code drops descriptions starting with the skills you invoke least, so the skills you use most keep their full text.

claim: To fit more skills, raise skillListingBudgetFraction or SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET, set low-priority skills to name-only in skillOverrides, or trim description and when_to_use at the source.
why: Each entry costs context on every turn whether or not the skill is used.
check: Look for skillOverrides entries and unused skills with long descriptions; a set with many long descriptions and no overrides is a problem.
quote: To free budget for other skills, set low-priority entries to

claim: In Claude Code all skill frontmatter fields are optional and only description is recommended; unknown or misspelled fields are silently ignored.
why: A typo in a field name produces no error, so the intended setting just does not apply.
check: Compare each skill's frontmatter keys to the documented list; flag misspelled or invented keys (for example camelCase or underscores) that do nothing.
quote: A field name must match the table exactly, hyphens included: Claude Code ignores a field it doesn't recognize without reporting an error.

claim: If a Claude Code skill has no description, the first non-empty line of the markdown body is used as its description.
why: The description is what Claude routes on, so an omitted one makes routing depend on whatever the body happens to start with.
check: Flag skills without a description field, especially model-invocable ones whose first body line is a heading or boilerplate.
quote: If omitted, uses the first non-empty line of the markdown content.

claim: Frontmatter is parsed only if the opening --- is the very first line of SKILL.md, otherwise the entire file including the markers becomes skill content; invalid YAML loads the skill with no fields set.
why: Either failure leaves the skill without a description, so /skill-name works but Claude cannot match it.
check: Check that each SKILL.md starts with --- on line 1 and parses (claude plugin validate can find unparseable files); flag leading blank lines, BOMs or comments.
quote: Claude Code reads the frontmatter only when the opening `---` is the file's first line. Otherwise it treats the whole file, `---` markers included, as skill content.

claim: Malformed skill YAML does not stop the skill loading: it loads with empty metadata, so direct invocation works but description-based matching does not.
why: The failure is silent in normal use and only visible with --debug.
check: If a skill never triggers automatically but runs when typed, suspect a frontmatter parse error.
quote: If the frontmatter YAML is malformed, Claude Code loads the skill body with empty metadata, so `/skill-name` still works but Claude can't match against your `description`.

claim: when_to_use is an optional field appended to description in the listing and it counts toward the same 1,536-character cap.
why: It is a place for trigger phrases and example requests, not extra budget.
check: Check that when_to_use is not duplicating description and that the combined length stays under the cap.
quote: Appended to `description` in the skill listing and counts toward the 1,536-character cap.

claim: disable-model-invocation: true stops Claude from invoking a skill on its own and, per the invocation table, removes its description from context; it is meant for workflows with side effects or manual timing like commit or deploy.
why: You do not want Claude deciding to deploy because the code looks ready.
check: Flag skills with side effects (deploy, commit, send message, delete) that leave model invocation enabled; flag purely manual skills that still pay description cost.
quote: **`disable-model-invocation: true`**: Claude can't invoke the skill on its own. Use this for workflows with side effects or that you want to control timing

claim: disable-model-invocation: true removes the skill from Claude's context entirely, which also saves its listing cost.
why: Hidden skills add nothing to the per-turn listing.
check: For user-only workflows, check disable-model-invocation is set so description tokens are not spent.
quote: **Hide individual skills** by adding `disable-model-invocation: true` to their frontmatter. This removes the skill from Claude's context entirely.

claim: user-invocable: false hides a skill from the user but Claude can still invoke it; to stop Claude too, disable-model-invocation must be set.
why: The two fields control different parties; user-invocable false is for background knowledge.
check: Flag skills that use user-invocable: false expecting them to be unreachable by Claude.
quote: With `user-invocable: false`, you can't invoke the skill, but Claude still can.

claim: allowed-tools pre-approves tools only for the turn that invokes the skill and does not restrict which tools are available.
why: It is a permission grant, not a sandbox; every tool stays callable and permission settings still govern unlisted tools.
check: Flag skills that rely on allowed-tools as a restriction, and skills needing session-long approval that should use permission allow rules instead.
quote: It does not restrict which tools are available: every tool remains callable

claim: The allowed-tools grant clears when the user sends the next message, even though the skill text stays in context.
why: Instructions persist but permissions do not, so multi-turn skills will prompt again.
check: Check long multi-turn skills that depend on pre-approved Bash patterns for prompts mid-task.
quote: The grant clears when you send your next message.

claim: A project skill's allowed-tools applies even in a -p run in a folder never trusted, so skills checked into a repository can grant themselves broad tool access.
why: Repository content is untrusted input and the field is honored regardless of the trust dialog.
check: Review allowed-tools of repository skills for broad patterns such as Bash(*) or unrestricted Write.
quote: A skill can grant itself broad tool access, so review the `allowed-tools` of skills checked into a repository before you run Claude Code there.

claim: disallowed-tools removes tools from Claude's pool while a skill is active and clears on the next user message.
why: It lets autonomous skills avoid tools such as AskUserQuestion.
check: For background or loop skills, check whether interactive tools are disallowed.
quote: Tools removed from Claude's available pool while this skill is active.

claim: The model and effort frontmatter fields override only for the rest of the current turn and are not saved; with context: fork they set the forked subagent's model and effort instead.
why: The session model resumes on the next prompt.
check: Check model/effort overrides match the skill's difficulty (cheap model for mechanical skills) and that fork skills do not assume a session-wide switch.
quote: The override applies for the rest of the current turn and isn't saved to settings. The session model resumes when you send your next prompt.

claim: A skill's hooks frontmatter registers hooks when the skill is invoked and keeps them running for the rest of the session.
why: This keeps an every-time rule bundled with the skill that needs it.
check: Where a skill says 'always' or 'never' about an action, check whether a hook enforces it instead of prose.
quote: Hooks that Claude Code registers when the skill is invoked and keeps running for the rest of the session.

claim: The paths frontmatter limits automatic activation to when Claude works with files matching the globs, relative to the current working directory.
why: It narrows a skill's relevance, and files outside the working directory do not match.
check: Check file-type-specific skills for paths globs, and check globs are not defeated by worktrees or sibling directories.
quote: When set, Claude loads the skill automatically only when working with files matching the patterns.

claim: context: fork runs a skill in a new subagent that does not see the conversation history, so the skill body must be self-contained.
why: The skill content becomes the subagent's prompt and nothing else from the chat is passed.
check: For fork skills, verify the body states the full task and inputs; flag fork skills that only contain guidelines or refer to the earlier conversation.
quote: The subagent doesn't see your conversation history, so the skill's instructions have to stand on their own.

claim: A context: fork skill containing only guidelines and no task returns without meaningful output.
why: The subagent receives guidelines but no actionable prompt.
check: Flag reference-style skills (conventions, style guides) that set context: fork.
quote: `context: fork` only makes sense for skills with explicit instructions.

claim: A forked skill using agent: Explore starts with only the skill content and that agent's own system prompt, with none of the CLAUDE.md files.
why: Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md to keep context small, so everything the task needs must be in SKILL.md.
check: For fork skills with agent Explore or Plan, check that project conventions they depend on are in the skill body.
quote: A forked skill using `agent: Explore` starts with that content and the agent's own system prompt, and none of your CLAUDE.md files.

claim: A forked skill runs in the background by default (background: true) and a backgrounded fork has a narrower tool set; background: false waits for the result and keeps the full tool set.
why: Skills whose steps need tools outside the background subset fail silently otherwise.
check: Check fork skills that need Edit, Bash or other tools for background: false.
quote: Set `background: false` in the frontmatter to instead wait for the result in the turn that invoked the skill.

claim: In a skill, a failing !`command` injection aborts the whole invocation and Claude never sees the skill content.
why: Dynamic context is rendered before Claude reads the skill, and any non-zero exit (other than exit 1 from search tools) counts as failure.
check: Check skills with ! commands for guards such as || true on commands that may exit non-zero.
quote: A failed command aborts the entire skill invocation, not just its own placeholder. Claude never sees the skill content for that invocation.

claim: The inline !`cmd` syntax is only recognized at the start of a line or after whitespace; elsewhere (for example KEY=!`cmd`) it stays literal text and the command does not run.
why: Placement rules decide whether injection happens.
check: Scan injected commands in skills for placements that would not expand.
quote: The inline form is only recognized when `!` appears at the start of a line or immediately after whitespace.

claim: When a skill is invoked its rendered SKILL.md enters the conversation as one message that stays for later turns and is not re-read from disk.
why: Because the content persists, every line is a recurring token cost, and guidance should be phrased as standing instructions rather than one-time steps.
check: Check skill bodies for one-shot phrasing ('run the tests') where a standing rule ('run the tests after every edit') is meant.
quote: Claude Code does not re-read the skill file on later turns, so write guidance that should apply throughout a task as standing instructions rather than one-time steps.

claim: After auto-compaction, Claude Code re-attaches only the first 5,000 tokens of each invoked skill, within a combined 25,000-token budget filled from the most recently invoked skill.
why: Older or later parts of long skills can be lost, so critical instructions must sit at the top.
check: Flag SKILL.md files over about 5,000 tokens with critical rules placed late; flag workflows that chain many large skills in one session.
quote: Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill after the summary, keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each. Re-attached skills share a combined budget of 25,000 tokens.

claim: Rules that must hold every time should move from a skill into a hook; judgment guidance should be worded to cover the whole task.
why: Claude may stop following a skill mid-session, whereas Claude Code runs hooks every time the event occurs.
check: Flag skills containing must-always or must-never rules that have no hook backing them.
quote: put the most important instructions near the top of `SKILL.md`.

claim: Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and move detailed reference material into separate supporting files referenced from SKILL.md.
why: Supporting files load only when needed, so large references cost nothing until used.
check: Flag SKILL.md files over 500 lines, and supporting files that SKILL.md never mentions.
quote: Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files.

claim: Skill bodies should state what to do rather than narrate how or why, applying the same conciseness test as CLAUDE.md.
why: Once loaded, the content stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost.
check: Flag skill bodies with long background explanations or content Claude would do anyway.
quote: State what to do rather than narrating how or why, and apply the same conciseness test you would for

claim: Procedures that have grown inside CLAUDE.md should become skills, because a skill's body loads only when used.
why: Always-loaded CLAUDE.md content costs tokens every session, whereas a skill costs almost nothing until needed.
check: Look in CLAUDE.md for step-by-step procedures or long reference sections that could be skills.
quote: Unlike CLAUDE.md content, a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.

claim: Same-named skills are resolved enterprise over personal over project; a plugin skill never collides because it is namespaced plugin-name:skill-name; skills override built-in commands but not their aliases.
why: Where each came from decides which one /name runs.
check: Look for duplicate skill names across scopes and for project skills shadowed by personal ones.
quote: Enterprise over personal, and personal over project.

claim: Project skills are loaded from .claude/skills/ in the start directory and every parent up to the repo root, while skills in subdirectories below the start directory load only when Claude first reads or edits a file there.
why: Nested skills are not in the listing at startup and cannot be invoked by name until loaded.
check: For monorepos, check where skills live relative to where sessions start.
quote: Skills in a `.claude/skills/` directory below where you started don't load at startup. They load the first time Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory

claim: Custom commands in .claude/commands/ have merged into skills and still work, with the same frontmatter except name and paths; skills are preferred because they support supporting files.
why: Commands cannot carry multiple files.
check: Flag commands directories holding multi-file procedures that should be skills.
quote: **Custom commands have been merged into skills.** Your existing `.claude/commands/` files keep working.

claim: Claude Code skills accept every frontmatter field, but claude.ai uploads and the Skills API accept only name, description, license, compatibility, metadata and allowed-tools, and fail with a hard error on any other field.
why: Fields like argument-hint, disable-model-invocation or context are Claude Code extensions that break packaging for other surfaces.
check: If a skill is meant to be shared to claude.ai or the API, check that its frontmatter uses only the six spec fields.
quote: If you include any field the spec doesn't allow, packaging or upload fails with a hard error instead of ignoring the field:

claim: The license, compatibility and metadata frontmatter fields are accepted by Claude Code but have no effect on its behavior.
why: They exist for the Agent Skills spec and the author's own tooling.
check: Do not credit these fields as functional configuration.
quote: Claude Code doesn't act on its contents, and drops a value that isn't a map.

claim: Angle brackets in description and when_to_use are shown as < and >, so placeholders should use square brackets or argument-hint.
why: The text is sanitized so it cannot imitate internal formatting.
check: Flag descriptions that use <placeholder> syntax.
quote: Claude Code displays `<` and `>` in the `description` and `when_to_use` fields as `<` and `>`.

claim: If a skill is invoked with arguments but its body has no placeholder, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: followed by the input to the end of the content.
why: Claude still sees what the user typed.
check: Check skills documented as taking arguments for $ARGUMENTS, $N or named placeholders and an argument-hint.
quote: If you invoke a skill with arguments but no placeholder in the skill's content receives one, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <your input>` to the end of the skill content

claim: Use ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} in both the skill body and an allowed-tools Bash rule so a bundled script runs without a permission prompt and regardless of working directory.
why: The rule then matches the exact command the body tells Claude to run.
check: Flag skills that hardcode absolute or relative script paths instead of the substitution variable.
quote: Using the same variable in both places lets a skill run a bundled script without a permission prompt.

claim: In a regular session only skill descriptions are in context and the full skill loads on invoke, but subagents with preloaded skills get the full content injected at startup.
why: Preloading trades context for guaranteed availability.
check: Check subagents that preload skills for large skill bodies that inflate every run.
quote: In a regular session, skill descriptions are loaded into context so Claude knows what's available, but full skill content only loads when invoked.

claim: Every skill in the listing costs context on every turn whether or not it is used; /skill-doctor reports per-skill cost and usage and flags never-invoked skills.
why: Unused skills are pure overhead.
check: Run or ask for /skill-doctor output; flag never-used skills, highest cost first.
quote: Run `/skill-doctor` to see what each of your skills costs and how often it gets used, so you can decide which ones to turn off.

claim: Evaluate a skill by running realistic prompts in a fresh session with the skill and with it turned off and comparing; trigger and output quality are measured separately.
why: Seeing a skill trigger only shows Claude found it, and leftover authoring context masks gaps.
check: Ask whether the skill author has a baseline comparison or any trigger evals; absence is a gap.
quote: Seeing a skill trigger tells you Claude found it, not that it did what you intended.

claim: The skill-creator plugin can tune a description by generating should-trigger and should-not-trigger prompts, measuring hit rate and proposing edits.
why: Description quality determines routing and is measurable.
check: For skills that trigger wrongly or not at all, check whether description tuning has been run.
quote: generates should-trigger and should-not-trigger prompts, measures the hit rate, and proposes description edits when the skill activates on the wrong requests

claim: When a skill does not trigger, first check that the description contains keywords users would naturally say; when it triggers too often, make the description more specific or set disable-model-invocation.
why: Description text is the only routing signal Claude has.
check: Compare each description against realistic phrasings of the requests it should serve.
quote: Check the description includes keywords users would naturally say

claim: skillOverrides has four states (on, name-only, user-invocable-only, off) and does not apply to plugin skills.
why: It controls visibility without editing a shared SKILL.md.
check: For shared repo skills with heavy descriptions, check skillOverrides is used; do not expect it to affect plugin skills.
quote: Plugin skills are not affected by `skillOverrides`. Manage those through `/plugin` instead.

claim: In the platform docs, name and description are the required skill fields; name is at most 64 characters, lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only, with no XML tags and no reserved words anthropic or claude.
why: These are validation rules on the API and claude.ai; the Claude Code docs instead say every field is optional and name defaults to the directory name, so the two doc sets differ.
check: Check each skill has name and description if it may ship beyond Claude Code, and that names meet the character and reserved-word rules.
quote: `name`: Maximum 64 characters, lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens only, no XML tags, no reserved words

claim: The platform docs cap description at 1,024 characters, non-empty and without XML tags, whereas Claude Code docs cap the listing text (description plus when_to_use) at 1,536 characters.
why: The two limits differ, so a description valid in Claude Code can be rejected by the API and claude.ai upload.
check: For skills that must also be uploaded elsewhere, keep description at or under 1,024 characters.
quote: `description`: Maximum 1,024 characters, non-empty, no XML tags

claim: The platform overview says Required fields are name and description, while the Claude Code doc says all fields are optional with only description recommended.
why: This is a disagreement between official doc sets; Claude Code tolerates what the platform rejects.
check: Do not fail a Claude Code-only skill for missing name, but do flag it if it will be uploaded elsewhere.
quote: **Required fields:** `name` and `description`

claim: At startup the name and description of every installed skill are loaded into the system prompt, and the description is what Claude matches requests against, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it.
why: Only the metadata is always in context, which lets many skills be installed without a context penalty.
check: Check each description states both capability and trigger conditions, not just a topic.
quote: The `description` is what Claude matches your request against when determining whether to trigger the Skill, so it must say both what the Skill does and when to use it.

claim: Write descriptions in third person, because the description is injected into the system prompt and inconsistent point of view can cause discovery problems.
why: The source gives this as the reason; first-person or second-person phrasing ('I can help', 'You can use this') is called out as wrong.
check: Flag descriptions beginning with 'I', 'You can' or 'Use this to' written as an address to the user.
quote: **Always write in third person**. The description is injected into the system prompt, and inconsistent point-of-view can cause discovery problems.

claim: A good description names concrete capabilities and specific triggers or key terms; vague descriptions such as 'Helps with documents' fail.
why: Claude picks among potentially 100+ skills by description alone, while the body only supplies implementation detail.
check: Flag descriptions lacking file types, verbs, domain terms or an explicit 'Use when' clause.
quote: The description is critical for skill selection: Claude uses it to choose the right Skill from potentially 100+ available Skills.

claim: Prefer descriptive, consistent skill names, ideally gerund form such as processing-pdfs, and avoid vague names (helper, utils, tools), overly generic ones (documents, data) and reserved words.
why: Consistent names make skills easier to reference, understand and organize as a collection.
check: Review the set's names for vague words and inconsistent patterns.
quote: Consider using **gerund form** (verb + -ing) for Skill names

claim: Skills use three levels of progressive disclosure: metadata always loaded, SKILL.md body loaded when triggered, and bundled files and script output loaded only as needed, with scripts' code never entering context.
why: This lets bundled content be effectively unbounded without a context penalty.
check: Check that heavy content lives in referenced files or scripts rather than the SKILL.md body.
quote: until a Skill is triggered, only its name and description occupy context

claim: Keep the SKILL.md body under 500 lines and split into separate files when approaching that limit.
why: It is given as optimal for performance, and once loaded every token competes with conversation history.
check: Flag long SKILL.md files; the Claude Code doc gives the same 500-line figure.
quote: Keep the `SKILL.md` body under 500 lines for optimal performance.

claim: Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md, linking every reference file directly from SKILL.md.
why: Claude may only preview files referenced from other referenced files (for example head -100) and so read them incompletely.
check: Flag reference chains where SKILL.md links to a file that links to another.
quote: **Keep references one level deep from `SKILL.md`**. All reference files should link directly from `SKILL.md` to ensure Claude reads complete files when needed.

claim: Reference files longer than 100 lines should start with a table of contents.
why: It lets Claude see the full scope even when it reads only part of the file.
check: Check long reference files for a contents list at the top.
quote: For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top.

claim: Only add context Claude does not already have; challenge each paragraph for whether it justifies its token cost.
why: The context window is shared with the system prompt, history and other skills' metadata.
check: Flag skill bodies that explain common knowledge (what a PDF is, how libraries work).
quote: Only add context Claude doesn’t already have.

claim: Match instruction specificity to fragility: high freedom for context-dependent tasks, low freedom (exact scripts, few parameters) for fragile operations like migrations.
why: A narrow bridge needs guardrails; an open field needs only direction.
check: Check that fragile or destructive steps are scripted exactly and flexible tasks are not over-prescribed.
quote: Match the level of specificity to the task’s fragility and variability.

claim: Test a skill with every model it will run on, since what works for Opus may need more detail for Haiku; Opus tends to need less over-explanation.
why: Skills are additions to the model, so effectiveness depends on the model underneath.
check: Check whether the skill was tried on the smaller models in use; the source's model list here is Haiku, Sonnet, Opus.
quote: What works perfectly for Opus might need more detail for Haiku.

claim: Prefer pre-made scripts for deterministic operations and state whether Claude should run a script or read it as reference.
why: Scripts are more reliable than generated code, save tokens, and only their output enters context.
check: Check bundled scripts are referenced with explicit run-or-read intent and fail with helpful errors rather than deferring to Claude.
quote: For most utility scripts, execution is preferred because it’s more reliable and efficient.

claim: Build evaluations before writing extensive skill documentation: find gaps without the skill, make at least three scenarios, baseline, then write minimal instructions.
why: It ensures the skill solves real problems rather than imagined ones.
check: Ask whether the skill has any evaluation scenarios; the checklist expects at least three.
quote: **Create evaluations BEFORE writing extensive documentation.**

claim: Avoid time-sensitive information in skills, putting superseded material in a collapsed old patterns section.
why: Date-conditional instructions become wrong.
check: Flag skills with date-dependent branches.
quote: Don’t include information that will become outdated:

claim: Give one default approach with an escape hatch instead of listing many alternative tools, use forward-slash paths, and reference MCP tools as ServerName:tool_name.
why: Too many options confuse Claude; Windows paths fail on Unix; unqualified MCP names can cause tool-not-found errors.
check: Flag 'use A or B or C' instructions, backslash paths and bare MCP tool names.
quote: Don’t present multiple approaches unless necessary:

claim: The platform docs say custom skills do not sync across surfaces, while Claude Code docs describe skills enabled on a claude.ai account being downloaded into Claude Code sessions.
why: The sources disagree; the Claude Code page is the more specific and detailed account, but the platform overview still states the separation.
check: When auditing skill distribution, check which surface each skill is actually available on.
quote: **Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces**.

claim: Skills synced from claude.ai are downloaded only, never uploaded, so edits under ~/.claude/skills/synced/ are overwritten by later syncs.
why: The account copy is the source of truth.
check: Flag local edits to synced skills.
quote: Claude Code downloads synced skills and never uploads them.

claim: Use skills only from trusted sources and audit all bundled files, scripts and external URL fetches before use.
why: A malicious skill can direct Claude to call tools or run code that does not match its stated purpose.
check: Review third-party or repo-sourced skills for network calls, odd file access and fetched instructions.
quote: Use Skills only from trusted sources: those you created yourself or obtained from Anthropic.

claim: Pay particular attention to a skill's name and description since Claude uses them when deciding whether to trigger it, and iterate by observing real Claude usage.
why: The engineering post presents metadata as the first level of progressive disclosure.
check: Check descriptions were revised after observing real triggering behavior.
quote: Pay special attention to the name and description of your skill.

claim: Keep mutually exclusive or rarely co-used contexts in separate files so they are not loaded together.
why: Separate paths reduce token usage.
check: Check that SKILL.md branches into separate files by scenario rather than combining them.
quote: If certain contexts are mutually exclusive or rarely used together, keeping the paths separate will reduce the token usage.

claim: The platform docs say there is no built-in way to run skill evaluations, while Claude Code has skill-creator and claude plugin eval.
why: The sources are from different doc sets and the platform page predates the Claude Code tooling.
check: Do not tell users there is no eval tooling; point to claude plugin eval for plugin skills and skill-creator otherwise.
quote: There is not currently a built-in way to run these evaluations.

claim: An output style is a set of instructions for role, tone and format that applies to every response in a session, and is a plain instruction with no enforcement.
why: It cannot guarantee behavior; use CLAUDE.md for project knowledge, a hook for guarantees, and a skill for task-specific procedures.
check: Flag output styles used to enforce rules, or used for project facts that belong in CLAUDE.md.
quote: An output style applies to every response in a session. It's an instruction Claude follows, so nothing enforces it.

claim: Custom output styles drop Claude Code's built-in software engineering instructions on the full system prompt unless keep-coding-instructions: true is set (default false).
why: A style that only changes tone would otherwise remove guidance on scoping changes, comments and verification.
check: For custom styles in coding setups, check keep-coding-instructions: true is set unless a non-coding role is intended.
quote: On the full system prompt, custom output styles leave out Claude Code's section of built-in software engineering instructions, such as how to scope changes, write comments, and verify work, unless `keep-coding-instructions` is set to `true`.

claim: On the shorter system prompt, keep-coding-instructions has no effect because that section is not included there.
why: The full prompt must be selected (CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0) to rely on the field.
check: Do not assume the field matters on setups using the shorter prompt.
quote: The shorter system prompt doesn't include that section, so the field has no effect there.

claim: Output styles apply to the main conversation and conversation forks, but not to other subagents.
why: Other subagents run their own system prompt.
check: Do not expect a style to change subagent output; put format rules in the subagent's own prompt.
quote: so styles don't change how they respond.

claim: The outputStyle setting value is case-sensitive, and a non-matching value silently gives the Default style.
why: Only the /output-style command ignores case.
check: Check outputStyle in settings files matches a style name exactly.
quote: A value that doesn't match a style name exactly, such as `explanatory`, gives you the Default style.

claim: Custom output style files are read when the terminal session starts, so edits need a restart, and unknown frontmatter fields are ignored (fields: name, description, keep-coding-instructions, force-for-plugin).
why: There is no live reload for styles unlike skills.
check: Check styles use only the four documented fields.
quote: In the terminal, Claude Code reads style files when it starts, so if you create or edit one during a running session, restart Claude Code to pick up the change.

claim: A style's instructions are sent with every request, adding input tokens (reduced by prompt caching); Explanatory and Learning raise output tokens, Concise lowers them.
why: Styles are always-on, unlike skills.
check: Weigh a custom style's length against its value, since it is paid on every request.
quote: A style's instructions add input tokens, though prompt caching reduces this cost after the first request in a session.

claim: Output styles differ from skills in that a skill loads only when invoked or when the task matches, so it does not shape unrelated responses, while a style shapes every response.
why: The docs' own comparison table makes this the deciding factor between the two.
check: Flag task-specific procedures written as output styles, and always-on voice rules written as skills.
quote: Claude loads it only when you invoke it or the task matches, so it doesn't shape unrelated responses

claim: Plugin output styles with force-for-plugin: true apply automatically whenever the plugin is enabled and override the user's outputStyle setting.
why: It lets a plugin impose a style; if several do, the first loaded wins.
check: Flag plugins that force an output style, since they override user choice.
quote: Set to `true` to apply this style automatically whenever the plugin is enabled, without requiring users to select it. Overrides the user's `outputStyle` setting.

claim: A Claude Code plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers or other components installed and loaded as one unit, usually with a manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json.
why: Packaging lets a setup be shared, versioned and updated together.
check: Check whether a plugin bundles related components or is a grab bag.
quote: A Claude Code plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, or other components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit.

claim: A plugin is warranted when several components are packaged as one unit or shared across machines; standalone skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers work without one.
why: Plugins add install, versioning and per-session overhead that a single personal skill does not need.
check: Flag one-skill plugins used only locally.
quote: Use a plugin when you want several skills, subagents, hooks, or MCP servers packaged as one unit.

claim: An enabled plugin adds the name and description of each model-invocable skill, agent and command to context on every turn, in every session, even when nothing from it runs.
why: Claude needs to know the components exist; the full text loads only on use.
check: List enabled plugins and flag those unused or with many long descriptions.
quote: the name and description are in Claude's context on every turn so that Claude knows it exists.

claim: A plugin manifest is optional and only name is required in it; Claude Code loads a plugin without a manifest.
why: The manifest carries metadata and userConfig, not the components themselves.
check: Do not treat a missing plugin.json as broken; check name and version in published plugins.
quote: Claude Code loads a plugin without one. Inside the file, only `name` is required.

claim: Plugin skills live in skills/<dir>/SKILL.md and run as /<plugin>:<directory>; a frontmatter name replaces only the last segment.
why: Namespacing avoids collisions with local skills.
check: Check plugin skill directory names are meaningful since they form the command.
quote: **Command name**: `/<plugin>:<directory>`, so `skills/review/SKILL.md` in `my-plugin` is `/my-plugin:review`.

claim: Claude Code does not load a CLAUDE.md at a plugin's root; instructions in a plugin must be written as a skill.
why: Plugins have no always-on instruction channel apart from skills and hooks.
check: Flag plugins that ship CLAUDE.md expecting it to load; claude plugin validate warns about it.
quote: To include instructions in a plugin, write them as a skill. Claude Code doesn't load a `CLAUDE.md` at the plugin root

claim: New plugin work should use skills rather than the older commands/ format, and rules that must hold every time belong in a hook rather than a skill.
why: Skills can carry supporting files; hooks run regardless of whether Claude follows instructions.
check: Flag plugins built on commands/ and plugins using skills for must-always rules.
quote: Commands are the older format: a skill runs by name the same way and can also carry supporting files in its own directory, so write new ones as skills

claim: Plugin hooks register when a session loads the plugin and fire on their events regardless of whether any of the plugin's skills are used.
why: Enabling a plugin means its hooks and MCP servers run in every session.
check: Review plugin hooks' matchers for breadth, since they run all the time.
quote: A plugin's hooks don't wait for one of the plugin's skills or commands to be used.

claim: Plugin agent files ignore the frontmatter fields permissionMode, hooks, mcpServers and initialPrompt.
why: A plugin agent cannot add hooks or MCP servers itself; those go in plugin-level hooks and .mcp.json.
check: Flag plugin agents declaring these fields expecting them to work.
quote: **Ignored fields**: `permissionMode`, `hooks`, `mcpServers`, and `initialPrompt`.

claim: Plugins reference their own files via ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, which changes on every update, and keep state in ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, which survives updates.
why: Each version has its own cache directory.
check: Flag plugins writing state under the root or hardcoding install paths.
quote: a directory that survives updates, for `node_modules`, virtual environments, and caches.

claim: Files in a plugin's bin/ directory are put on PATH after the user's own entries, so a plugin cannot shadow system commands.
why: It prevents plugins overriding git or ls.
check: Check bin/ scripts have unique names and are executable.
quote: Plugin `bin/` directories come after the user's own `PATH` entries, so a plugin can't shadow `git`, `ls`, or another system command.

claim: Plugins can ship output styles (as <plugin>:<name>) and color themes, and plugin themes are read-only.
why: They appear in the same pickers as the user's own.
check: Check plugin output styles set keep-coding-instructions appropriately.
quote: A plugin can include color themes and output styles. Both appear in the same pickers as the user's own.

claim: A marketplace operator can add a relevance block (topic and signals: cwd, cli, hosts, filesRead, manifestDeps) so Claude Code suggests the plugin, and it never installs it automatically.
why: Suggestions are prompts; the user always confirms.
check: For org marketplaces, check relevance signals are present and narrow enough to avoid noisy suggestions.
quote: Claude Code never installs the plugin automatically. The user always confirms.

claim: Relevance signal matching happens locally with no network traffic and no reporting of matched signals to Anthropic or the marketplace operator.
why: It is a privacy property of the feature.
check: Relevant when advising on privacy concerns about suggestions.
quote: Signal matching happens locally on the user's machine and adds no network traffic.

claim: In the terminal, plugin suggestions from a marketplace do not appear until an administrator allowlists it in managed settings via pluginSuggestionMarketplaces, with a source declaration for non-official marketplaces.
why: The source check stops an unrelated source from registering under an allowlisted name.
check: If an org marketplace has relevance blocks but users see no suggestions, check managed settings.
quote: In the terminal, users see no suggestions from a marketplace until an administrator allowlists it in

claim: Only the cwd relevance signal can match at session start, and the cli signal records only the leading command of each shell command, so cd infra && terraform plan records cd.
why: These matching rules decide whether a signal can ever fire.
check: Check cli signals do not depend on commands usually run second in a compound command.
quote: Compound commands contribute only their leading command, so `cd infra && terraform plan` records `cd`, not `terraform`.

claim: A relevance field that exceeds its documented limit invalidates the whole plugin entry so it cannot be installed from the marketplace; claude plugin validate reports the limits.
why: Limits are enforced strictly for recognized fields.
check: Run claude plugin validate on the marketplace before publishing.
quote: invalidates the whole plugin entry, and users can't install that plugin from the marketplace until you fix it

claim: A given plugin suggestion appears at most once every three sessions, and the session-start notification stops after a combined two showings.
why: It limits suggestion fatigue.
check: Do not expect repeated nudges when evaluating relevance effectiveness.
quote: The suggestion appears at most once every three sessions across the spinner tip and the session-start notification combined.

claim: claude plugin eval runs each case three times by default in an isolated non-interactive session with only the plugin loaded, and a case's score is the mean of its runs.
why: A single run of a non-deterministic agent tells little.
check: Check eval suites keep the default run count when making decisions, using fewer only to iterate.
quote: One run of a non-deterministic agent tells you little, so each case runs three times by default.

claim: Plugin evals compare each case with and without the plugin, giving WITH, W/OUT and a delta; a case scoring 1.0 in both shows the plugin did not cause the pass.
why: A high score alone does not show the plugin helped.
check: Look at delta, not just pass rate, when judging whether a plugin or skill adds value.
quote: If a case scores 1.0 both with and without the plugin, the plugin isn't what made it pass.

claim: To test whether a skill's description triggers, write the eval prompt as a user would type it without naming the skill and add a tool_used Skill grader; a near-zero delta with that grader failing means the description does not trigger on natural phrasing.
why: This is called the most common first finding in plugin evals.
check: Check eval prompts do not name the skill and that trigger cases include should-not-trigger prompts.
quote: The most common first finding is a `Δ` near zero with the case's `tool_used: Skill` grader failing, which means Claude isn't choosing your skill on natural phrasing.

claim: In two-arm eval runs, tool_used graders for the Skill tool are excluded from the score and shown only as plugin-fired indicators, because they cannot pass without the plugin.
why: Counting them would drag the baseline toward zero and inflate delta.
check: A passing Skill-fired indicator alone is not evidence of quality; look at the result graders.
quote: Every `tool_used` grader whose `tool` is `Skill`

claim: Give each eval case one grader on the result and one on the steps taken, use regex graders for long output, and keep llm graders for short outputs with concrete PASS and FAIL conditions.
why: LLM judge verdicts vary more as the text gets longer.
check: Check suites mix outcome and process graders and avoid LLM graders over large files.
quote: For long output such as a generated file, grade it with a `regex` grader over the file's contents

claim: Eval runs load no user settings, CLAUDE.md, hooks, other plugins, memory or personal skills, so everything a case depends on must ship inside the plugin under test.
why: Isolation keeps results repeatable.
check: Flag evals that rely on user or project configuration being present.
quote: **Nothing personal or project-level loads.**

claim: In CI, pin the agent model and judge model, use --threshold, --max-cost-usd and --trust-plugin, and note that the delta never changes the exit code.
why: Pinning stops a model rollout being mistaken for a plugin regression; every run and judge call is a paid model call.
check: Check CI eval jobs pin models and set a cost ceiling, and do not gate on delta.
quote: Pin it in CI so a model rollout isn't mistaken for a plugin regression

claim: The default eval threshold is 1.0, so any case below perfect makes the command exit 1.
why: Non-deterministic cases often score under 1.0, so the default can fail passing-looking suites.
check: Check CI thresholds are chosen deliberately.
quote: The with-minus-without delta is reported but never changes the exit code

claim: claude plugin eval has no custom-code graders; the types are regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists, llm and baseline.
why: Only the first four are free; llm and baseline call a judge model.
check: Budget for judge calls when suites use llm or baseline graders.
quote: There are no custom-code graders.

claim: The skill-creator plugin eval format (evals/evals.json) and claude plugin eval case files are not interchangeable.
why: Neither tool reads the other's case files.
check: Do not treat a skill-creator evals.json as a claude plugin eval suite.
quote: The two formats aren't interchangeable.

claim: claude plugin details reports a plugin's always-on token cost, counted from each component's name plus its description and when_to_use, and per-component on-invoke cost.
why: That always-on figure is what every user carries each session.
check: Run claude plugin details on installed plugins and flag high always-on totals.
quote: The always-on figure counts each component's name plus its `description` and `when_to_use` frontmatter.

claim: To lower a plugin's always-on cost, shorten descriptions or split the plugin, then recheck triggering with a Skill grader because a shorter description can stop the skill triggering.
why: Description is both the cost and the routing signal.
check: Check trimmed descriptions still trigger on realistic prompts.
quote: A skill's description is also what Claude matches a request against, so a shorter one can stop the skill triggering.

claim: Claude Code does not report plugin usage back to the plugin author; usage is recorded on each installer's machine and visible to admins through OpenTelemetry or the Analytics API.
why: Authors without admin access or a way to ask users have no usage signal.
check: For an author measuring use, check whether an OTel or Analytics API route is available.
quote: Claude Code doesn't report a plugin's usage back to its author.

claim: A marketplace-installed plugin moves to Not used recently in /plugin after at least 14 days and 10 sessions unused, but never for plugins that include a theme, output style, monitor or workflow, or those loaded by --plugin-dir or managed settings.
why: Those components are in use without a tracked invocation.
check: Do not read the absence of the header as evidence a plugin is used.
quote: once it has gone unused for at least 14 days and 10 sessions

claim: Official-marketplace plugins show a Context cost estimate before install, highlighted when the always-on figure is 2,000 tokens or more; plugins in your own marketplace show none.
why: It informs install decisions.
check: Treat 2,000 always-on tokens as the documented highlight threshold when flagging heavy plugins.
quote: When the always-on figure is 2,000 tokens or more, the `Every turn:` line appears highlighted.

claim: In plugin telemetry, third-party plugin names are redacted or omitted by default, including plugins from an organization's own marketplace, unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 is set.
why: Only the official marketplace's names are reported verbatim.
check: If fleet usage data shows third-party rows, check OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS before concluding usage is low.
quote: Every other plugin's name is redacted or omitted by default, including a plugin from your organization's own marketplace.
